title: Algebraic Characterization of k-Fold Origami Constructibility
description: Formalizes the conjectured algebraic characterization of k-fold origami constructibility: k simultaneous folds can construct exactly the p_{k+1}-smooth degrees (all prime factors ≤ the (k+1)-th prime). Proves strict hierarchy (each fold level adds one prime), monotonicity, and algebraic completeness (every degree is eventually constructible).

Strict hierarchy witnesses: 5 separates 1-fold from 2-fold, 7 separates 2-fold from 3-fold, 11 separates 3-fold from 4-fold

meta.assumptions: None. 0 axioms, 0 sorries. All results follow from the IsKFoldConstructible definition. The definition itself encodes the conjectured pattern for k ≥ 3 (which is mathematically open).

overview.historicalContext: The classical ruler-and-compass constructibility theorem (Gauss-Wantzel, 1837) characterizes constructible lengths via 2-power field extensions, explaining why angle trisection is impossible with classical tools. Origami (paper folding) strictly extends this: the Huzita-Hatori axioms, formalized in the 1990s, enable construction of cube roots and, as Alperin proved (2000) and Alperin-Lang systematized (2006), solve all cubic and quartic equations. Single-fold origami corresponds to 3-smooth degrees (field extensions of degree $2^a 3^b$) and two-fold origami to 5-smooth degrees ($2^a 3^b 5^c$). The natural conjecture is that each additional simultaneous fold unlocks the next prime: $k$-fold origami $\leftrightarrow$ $p_{k+1}$-smooth degrees, giving the hierarchy compass $\subsetneq$ 1-fold $\subsetneq$ 2-fold $\subsetneq$ 3-fold $\subsetneq \cdots$, each level solving polynomial equations of one higher prime degree. This conjecture for $k \geq 3$ remains open as of 2026.
overview.problemStatement: What is the precise algebraic characterization of $k$-fold origami constructibility for $k \geq 3$? Conjectured: $k$ simultaneous folds construct exactly the $p_{k+1}$-smooth degrees — those whose prime factors are all $\leq$ the $(k+1)$-th prime.
overview.text: Formalizes p-smooth numbers and k-fold origami constructibility. Proves the strict hierarchy: each fold level adds exactly one new prime as a constructible degree. Every degree is eventually constructible with enough folds.
overview.proofStrategy: Define IsSmooth and IsKFoldConstructible using Mathlib's Nat.nth for prime enumeration. Use concrete prime bounds (from Nat.Prime.Nth) for small k. Prove strict hierarchy by showing the (k+2)-th prime is (k+1)-fold constructible but not k-fold. Prove algebraic completeness using add_two_le_nth_prime.
keyInsights: The smooth number framework cleanly captures k-fold constructibility: $p$-smooth means all prime factors $\leq p$, so $k$-fold origami is exactly the set of $p_k$-smooth degrees
Each fold level adds exactly one new prime to the constructible set: $p_{k+1}$ separates $k$-fold from $(k+1)$-fold, and is itself the canonical witness for the strict hierarchy

Monotonicity uses Euclid's theorem (primes are infinite) via `Nat.nth_strictMono`: the key insight is that the abstract monotonicity proof works uniformly for all $k$ because the prime sequence is strictly increasing
Algebraic completeness uses the prime growth bound $p_n \geq n+2$: take $k = d$ to ensure all prime factors of $d$ (which are $\leq d$) are below the prime bound $p_d \geq d+2$

The 'verified' badge and 0 axioms reflect a subtle point: the definition *encodes the conjecture* as a definition, so the 24+ theorems prove internal consistency of the conjecture, not the conjecture itself — a distinction fundamental to formalized mathematics
prerequisites: Prime numbers and the infinitude of primes
Smooth numbers: integers whose prime factors are bounded
Prime counting functions and Nat.nth from Mathlib

sections.title: Smooth Numbers
sections.summary: Defines IsSmooth p n (n > 0 and all prime factors ≤ p). Proves four closure theorems: one_smooth, prime_smooth, smooth_mul, and not_smooth_of_large_prime.
sections.mathContext: A positive integer $n$ is **$p$-smooth** if every prime factor of $n$ is $\leq p$. The 3-smooth numbers are $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, \ldots\}$ (products of primes $\leq 3$, i.e., powers of 2 and 3). Also called 3-smooth, Hamming numbers, or regular numbers.

sections.title: k-Fold Origami Constructibility Definitions
sections.summary: Defines foldPrimeBound k = Nat.nth Prime k (0-indexed: k=1 gives 3, k=2 gives 5, k=3 gives 7, k=4 gives 11). Defines IsKFoldConstructible d k = (k ≥ 1 ∧ IsSmooth (foldPrimeBound k) d). Proves concrete prime bound values via Mathlib's nth_prime_k_eq_p lemmas.
sections.mathContext: The prime bound for fold level $k$ is $p_k$ (0-indexed Nat.nth): $k=1 \to 3$, $k=2 \to 5$, $k=3 \to 7$, $k=4 \to 11$. Degree $d$ is $k$-fold constructible iff $d$ is $p_k$-smooth. The k ≥ 1 requirement excludes 0-fold (2-smooth), which has no physical meaning.

sections.title: Degree Classification: Primes Separate Fold Levels
sections.summary: Classifies prime degrees at fold levels: 3 (1-fold), 5 (2-fold not 1-fold), 7 (3-fold not 2-fold), 11 (4-fold not 3-fold). Bundles into strict hierarchy witnesses: strict_hierarchy_1_2, strict_hierarchy_2_3, strict_hierarchy_3_4.
sections.mathContext: The separating primes: $5$ separates 1-fold from 2-fold ($5 > 3 = p_1$ but $5 \leq 5 = p_2$), $7$ separates 2-fold from 3-fold, $11$ separates 3-fold from 4-fold. Each fold level adds exactly one new prime to the constructible set.

sections.title: Monotonicity via nth_strictMono
sections.summary: Proves constructible_mono: k-fold ⊆ (k+1)-fold for all k. Uses Nat.nth_strictMono on the infinite set of primes (Euclid's theorem) to conclude p_k < p_{k+1}.
sections.mathContext: The abstract monotonicity: $p_k < p_{k+1}$ from strict monotonicity of the prime enumeration on any infinite set. This gives $q \leq p_k \Rightarrow q \leq p_{k+1}$, hence $p_k$-smooth $\Rightarrow$ $p_{k+1}$-smooth.

sections.title: Composite Degree Classification
sections.summary: Classifies composite degrees: 6=2·3 (1-fold), 9=3² (1-fold), 10=2·5 (2-fold not 1-fold), 30=2·3·5 (2-fold), 42=2·3·7 (3-fold not 2-fold). Uses prime_dvd_6 helper and recursive prime factor extraction.
sections.mathContext: $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ is 3-smooth, $9 = 3^2$ is 3-smooth, $10 = 2 \cdot 5$ is 5-smooth but not 3-smooth ($5 > 3$), $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ is 5-smooth, $42 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$ is 7-smooth but not 5-smooth ($7 > 5$).

sections.title: Algebraic Completeness
sections.summary: Proves every d > 0 is k-fold constructible for some k, taking k = d. Uses Nat.add_two_le_nth_prime: p_d ≥ d+2 > d ≥ any prime factor of d.
sections.mathContext: Since $p_n \geq n + 2$ (Mathlib `Nat.add\_two\_le\_nth\_prime`) and all prime factors of $d$ are $\leq d < d + 2 \leq p_d$, taking $k = d$ makes $d$ a $p_d$-smooth number, hence $d$-fold constructible.

sections.title: Summary and #check Statements
sections.summary: Summary comment listing all proved results: smooth number framework, k-fold definition, degree classifications, strict hierarchy witnesses, monotonicity, completeness. Followed by #check statements verifying all main definitions/theorems type-check correctly.
sections.mathContext: The file achieves: 0 axioms, 0 sorries, 24+ theorems. All results follow from the IsKFoldConstructible definition. The conjecture for k ≥ 3 is mathematically open; the definition encodes it and the theorems verify its internal consistency.

conclusion.summary: Formalizes the conjectured algebraic characterization of $k$-fold origami: $p_k$-smooth degrees (0-indexed prime enumeration). The definition encodes the conjecture; 24+ theorems verify its internal consistency (strict hierarchy witnesses, monotonicity, algebraic completeness). For $k=1,2$ this recovers Alperin-Lang 2006; for $k \geq 3$ the conjecture is mathematically open.
conclusion.implications: The smooth number characterization reveals a deep connection between origami fold complexity and the prime sieve: each fold level adds exactly one prime to the constructible set, making the hierarchy 1-fold ⊊ 2-fold ⊊ 3-fold ⊊ ··· a perfect mirror of the prime sequence. The algebraic completeness result shows this hierarchy eventually reaches all polynomial degrees — not just a dense subset. This formalization also demonstrates a powerful technique: encoding an open conjecture as a definition and proving its consequences, which (1) makes the conjecture precise, (2) verifies the conjecture's internal consistency, and (3) provides immediately useful theorems if the conjecture is later proved.
openQuestions: For $k \geq 3$, can the conjectured equivalence 'IsKFoldConstructible $d$ $k$ ↔ $d$ is realizable by $k$ simultaneous fold operations' be proved using the Huzita-Hatori axioms?
Is the smooth number characterization the only clean algebraic description, or are there equivalent characterizations via Galois theory or field extensions?
What is the minimum number of simultaneous folds needed to solve a generic equation of degree $n$ (equivalently, what is the smallest $k$ such that $n$ is $p_k$-smooth)?
